scenes.card: At last Odysseus tells the court his name, says his home is Ithaca, and begins the story of his journey.

subs.text: Book nine.
In the One-Eyed Giant's Cave.
Scene one.
Odysseus Names Himself.
Alcinous, mighty king, it is a fine thing to hear a singer such as this, whose voice is like a god's.
No moment is sweeter than when joy holds a whole people —
feasters ranged down the hall listening, the tables full of bread and meat, the steward pouring wine.
This seems to my own heart the fairest thing there is.
But you ask my name, and I will hide it no longer.
I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, known to all men for my cunning, and my fame goes up to heaven.
Odysseus describes Ithaca's rugged beauty and his longing to return.
Come then —
I will tell you the bitter homecoming Zeus gave me out of Troy.

subs.text: Scene two.
The Raid on the Cicones.
Ismarus is ours!
Share out the spoil and the women —
equal portions, no man cheated!
Not yet, captain!
The sheep are fat and the wine runs dark and sweet —
one more cup on the beach, and then we row!
Cicones from inland arrive in organized force and fight through the day.
Six benches from every ship stand empty when at dusk the fleet claws free —
glad to be alive, and grieving for the comrades left behind.

scenes.card: Some sailors eat the lotus, a plant that makes them forget home; Odysseus drags them weeping back to the ships.

subs.text: Scene three.
The Lotus-Eaters.
Nine days the north wind and the killing seas drive the ships off course, past Cythera,
off the edge of the known world.
On the tenth day they land where the Lotus-eaters dwell,
and three men go inland to learn what people eat bread in that country.
The Lotus-eaters plan no death for them.
They offer only the lotus, honey-sweet.
Those who taste it lose all desire for home.
Take them, though they weep —
bind them under the benches!
The rest of you aboard and to your oars now, before another man tastes the lotus and forgets his home.

subs.text: Scene four.
Goat Island and the Cyclops Coast.
The fleet comes then to a wooded island where wild goats breed and no plow has ever cut,
lying just across the water from the land of the Cyclopes.
In darkness the ships enter a sheltered harbor and rest.
At dawn they hunt the goats down the glens and feast until sundown —
and across the strait they see the smoke of the Cyclopes' fires, and hear voices, and the bleating of sheep.
Odysseus takes one ship and selects twelve men to investigate the neighboring people.

scenes.title: The Empty Cave
scenes.card: Odysseus and twelve men find a cave full of food; the men want to steal and run, but he insists on waiting.

subs.text: Scene five.
The Empty Cave.
The wine of Maron comes with us —
twelve men, follow me.
My heart says we go to meet a man of great strength, lawless and wild.
Look —
racks bending under cheeses, pens of lambs and kids, each age folded apart, and the pails swimming with whey.
A careful hand keeps this place.
Let us take the cheeses and drive the lambs and kids to the ship, they begged him —
take them and run for the salt water while we can.
No —
we wait.
I would see the master of this cave myself, and take the guest-gift that strangers are owed.
My men saw truer than I, and how much better it would have been to listen.

scenes.title: The First Killings
scenes.card: Odysseus asks for the kindness owed to guests, but Polyphemus scorns the gods and eats two of his men.

subs.text: Scene seven.
The First Killings.
We are Achaeans out of Troy, men of Agamemnon, whose fame is the widest now under heaven —
driven here by every wind on the wrong sea-roads.
We come to your knees, hoping the welcome due a guest.
Respect the gods, mighty one:
Zeus himself walks with strangers and avenges them.
You are a fool, stranger, or come from very far, to bid me fear your gods.
We Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus of the aegis —
we are stronger by far, and I spare no man for fear of heaven.
But tell me:
where did you moor that fine ship of yours —
far up the coast, or near?
Odysseus lies that Poseidon smashed it against the rocks.

subs.text: Scene eight.
The Name Nobody and the Stake.
Odysseus considers killing the sleeping giant but realizes the entrance stone would trap them forever.
At dawn Polyphemus eats two more men and leaves with the flock, sealing the cave again.
The olive trunk there —
his own club.
Cut it to a fathom, smooth it, harden the point in the fire.
He has given us our weapon himself.
The men hide the stake beneath dung and draw lots for four helpers.
Here, Cyclops —
drink wine on that man-flesh you have eaten, and learn what drink our ship carried.
You ask my name, and I will tell it for the guest-gift you promised:
Nobody is my name.
Nobody —
so my father and mother and all my friends call me.

subs.text: Scene nine.
The Blinding.
Give me more, freely —
and here is your gift, Nobody, to warm your heart:
I eat Nobody last, after all his friends.
There is my guest-gift to you.
Odysseus heats the stake until it glows and the chosen men drive it into the Cyclops's eye.
Odysseus twist it as blood and steam erupt.
Polyphemus wakes with a roar and tears it free.
What ails you, Polyphemus, that you wake the deathless night with screaming —
is some man stealing your flocks, or killing you by craft or force?
If Nobody harms you, alone as you are, it is sickness sent by Zeus, and cannot be helped —
pray to your father Poseidon.
Polyphemus gropes at the entrance while the men hide among the animals.

scenes.title: Escape beneath the Rams
scenes.card: The men escape by clinging to the bellies of sheep as the blind giant lets his flock out to graze.

subs.text: Scene ten.
Escape beneath the Rams.
At dawn Polyphemus opens the cave and feels every animal's back as it passes.
Odysseus binds three rams abreast for each man, suspending a sailor beneath the middle animal.
I took the great lead ram myself and hung beneath his belly, my hands twisted in that miracle of wool,
and dared not breathe.
Over my head the blind master mourned to him:
Sweet ram, why last from the cave today, you who were always first —
do you grieve for your master's eye?
Outside, the men release themselves, drive the flock to the ship, and row away.
Share out the flock, every man his portion —
and the great ram goes to Zeus, lord of the dark cloud, with the thighs burnt on the fire.

scenes.title: The Boast and the Curse
scenes.card: Safe on the water, Odysseus boasts his real name; Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon to make the homecoming late and lonely.

subs.text: Scene eleven.
The Boast and the Curse.
Cyclops!
It was no weak man's friends you ate in your hollow cave —
your evil deeds were bound to find you out!
You dared devour guests in your own house, and Zeus and the gods have paid you for it!
Polyphemus tears off a mountain peak and hurls it, driving a wave that nearly beaches the ship again.
Cyclops —
if any mortal ever asks who put out your eye so shamefully, tell him this:
it was Odysseus, sacker of cities, who blinded you —
Laertes's son, whose home is in Ithaca!
So the old prophecy comes home —
Telemus foretold I would lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus, and I watched all these years for a great man,
not this little worthless nothing who undid me with wine.
Hear me, Poseidon, dark-haired shaker of the earth, if I am truly your son:
grant that Odysseus, sacker of cities, never reach his home.
Or if he must, let him come late and broken, on a stranger's ship, all his comrades lost —
and find trouble waiting in his house.
A second rock misses as the ship escapes to the fleet.
